doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: First professional gig at 15 at a pizza parlor with banjo players
summary: Mays recounts playing with a father-son banjo team and a washtub bass at the Gay Nineties Pizza Parlor, earning ten dollars a night and learning by ear.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Oh that’s fascinating. So can you compare that with your first gig when you were 15?

When I was 15 I got called by some, a father-son team. They both played the banjo and they needed a pianist for their gig at the Gay Nineties Pizza Parlor in Pleasant Hills, California. I was going to high school in the East Bay area. And I didn’t know very many tunes. I didn’t know much about jazz. I had recently heard Earl “Fatha” Hines and the Miles Davis band in San Francisco which completely flipped me and turned my head around and opened my ears. But what they did, they gave me a fake book and they said learn “Jada,” “The World is Waiting for a Sunrise,” “K-K-K-Katie” and other gems, and there was a gut bucket player, that is a washtub overturned with a broomstick handle and

a cord, a clothesline cord. No tone to speak of but he had a good beat, and the two banjo players. That was my first professional gig and I think I kind of remember making ten bucks a night which was probably a lot of money in the late ‘50s.
Yeah. You could – when you got a car you could fill up your tank.
What do you think they meant when they said, “learn these tunes.” – what were they expecting from you? Accompaniment style or did you have to play the melody?

No, they handled the melody. They wanted me to keep time. So I locked in with the gut bucket player and – this was an upright piano with thumbtacks in the hammers to get that old barroom Western piano effect. And the two banjo players, father and son, were sitting up on top of the piano so I’m looking at their feet on the left and the right of me. And as I remember I just kept time and I did some rudimentary improvising. I was – I didn’t – I don’t know how they got my name and I don't know why they called me because I had very, very little experience playing that kind of music. I did have a lot of experience as an accompanist because I had played for the choir and singers in my father’s church and I had a little combo with a couple of guys, a trumpet player and a bass player. And I was doing some arranging for that group. Again I didn’t know what I was doing. I had no books, I had no instruction manuals like we have today. And it was just hit and miss. Try this, what sounds good. Well that sounds good, that doesn’t sound good, and why doesn’t it sound good, and I would just figure it out as a I went. So I think that started me on my self-taught, self-starter kind of way of learning.
